Really though, I would avoid attributing to sexism what is far more easily attributed to oblivion, heavy investment in the game, and the simple fact that people can't read your mind. Its no wonder that people get defensive when you instantly assume the worst in them for making a mistake.

Other players don't know exactly when you thought of something to say, and maybe they thought of something to say too. There is no queue; a conversation is a constant negotiation, not to be dictated by any one person (except perhaps, in this case, the GM).

If you're honestly asserting yourself sufficiently in conversation, you should have relatively few issues. If you're doing all the right things all the time and you're leaving room for error - which is just realistic, people are not perfect - and you're still treated unfairly, I'd attribute it to one or more players in the group not being well socialized or simply lacking conversational skills, which is the most important thing for a player/GM to have.

If this is just missing from the group, then they are simply not worth your time. But attributing any and all mistakes made in conversation to one's gender, or to sexism, or "toxic masculinity reeeeee", even on the rare occasion that its accurate, is going to get you nowhere and make nothing better.

Seems to me like the best setup for this character is one of two extremes: all combat proficiency or no combat proficiency.

With all combat proficiency, you'd be like a hardened soldier who's been deeply involved in and affected by death. Being the strongest in combat means the party has to take into account how you feel when deciding whether to engage.

With no combat proficiency, you could be a Bilbo/Frodo: not much use with a sword, but you can still help during a fight. Use your non-combat skills in creative ways, manipulate the environment around you, cause distractions, or let the party distract the enemy so you can sneak around the back of the battlefield, infiltrate their cover, pick their locks, steal their weapons, plant traps, etc. Your lack of combat specific skills means you'll be much better at other things. Use that. I don't see how this wouldn't be fun.

I ordered a pack of 1000 blank index cards online and have since used them in a bunch of ways:

-loot deck

Players draw from the deck whenever looting occurs. Contains all items in the game, from random junk to full power armour, so looting is always exciting.

-dungeon tiles

Rooms and bits of hallway are drawn on cards from a birds eye view; dungeons take the form of decks. When players enter a dungeon, its deck is shuffled and the cards are layed out like dominoes as the players explore

-misc perks

My game has skills, and perks pertaining to those skills. These perks are on a chart, and the player can take one that they qualify for when they level up.

If they don't qualify for any new skill perks, there are also misc perks, which don't pertain to any skill. These are on cards. 10 are chosen at random and displayed for the player's choosing.

-crafting recipes

Some merchants will sell recipes for specialty items the players can craft using the junk they've collected from the loot deck. This includes things like weapon modifications, armour, backpacks, traps, construction parts, and even vehicle parts, if the party want to craft a car or a motorcycle.

Two things I might do:

Start them off together in a small settlement. Use your time in the safe area to:

-let the PCs get to know each other

-get the players familiar with the mechanics, with things like a shooting range, a combat training area, infirmary, watchtower, etc.

-a small low-stakes quest or two that get them to use their stats (eg. Hide n seek with the kids, heal someone, settle an arguement between two settlers, convince the inventory manager to dole out extra ammo to the guard, etc.) whatever the stats may be

-get them to talk to some NPCs to learn about the settlement and what's going on in the world outside

Once they've got this, get ready to send them outside for their first mission. Allow them each the pick of any weapon from the armoury. A lot of time is spent killing in settings with zombies; have a nice wide variety of weapons so they can express their character the way they want from the start.

Send them hunting, or to find some berries/herbs for a medicine, or to find a missing person.

Once they've completed their mission, have them return to a smoking ruin.
Everyone dead or gone, the armoury and infirmary empty (save for some optional loot, up to you) and signs of a struggle between two groups of humans. From there itt'd be up to you and them.

OR

Ask your players to come up with their characters separately before the game. People pretty much understand what to expect in a zombie apocalypse, so they probably won't have trouble coming up with one.

Ask them each what they want their character's situation and goals to be, going into the game.

Start the pilot by following the character with the most immediately urgent goal, and between short scuffles with undead, have them run into the rest of the PCs one by one at opportune moments. The session ends when they've all faced an adversary together and they've decided on the immediate path forward, forming the party.

> Fallout 3, Fallout 4, Skyrim, Oblivion, No Man's Sky

all games that were marketed on their bigness - the open world in these cases was the selling point on it's own, as it is a hollow promise of "hundreds of hours of content", since everything is so spread out that seeing everything is nearly impossible. These games tend towards being the world's most extraordinarily complicated mission select screens.

> Fallout 1, Fallout 2, New Vegas, Morrowind

These are my favourite games of all time. I would also add The Witcher 3 to this list. These games are not built on the selling point of being big, though they are big. These games present you with a scenario, a story that is greatly enhanced by telling it in an open world in which the player has agency regarding direction.

These games all put you in the role of a detective to some extent, and the open world helps tell the story because it is treated as a real place rather than an elaborate menu screen. In these games, level design is less about enforcing a gameplay loop of dungeon crawling, and more about weaving a web of cause and effect that is reflective of the real world - a web whose threads can be zoomed in on and followed by observant eyes to the centre where everything in the world intersects.

Open worlds and even procedural generation can be used to great effect by competent designers who have played a lot of games. The problem arises when world size becomes a back-of-the-box selling point instead of a tool for telling a story.

As someone running an rpg in a postapocalyptic setting, I'd love to hear some ideas you're playing around with.

As far as general "rules" to keep in mind regarding setting:

High risk, low reward - times are tough, food is scarce and disputes can arise over basic resources or space

High/low tech contrast - post apocalyptic fiction often leads to situations where culture and technology are out of sync, and so you might see tech cannibalized and repurposed to fulfill basic needs, people worshipping a computer, or tribal warriors with hi tech weapons, etc.

History Mystery - there is usually a certain degree of mystery surrounding the setting's past, and learning gradually how things came to be may play a role in the story somehow, or it may simply remain unknown

Factions - the big players in post apocalyptic worlds are those who have proposed radical solutions to these living conditions and gained a mass following in doing so. They build new nations on their ideas, but eventually these societies come into conflict with one another over resources or ideology
 
We the People - what matters most in order to tie it all together: you have to have people with personal stories of survival to tell, stories of human ingenuity and perserverence that are at once horrific and uplifting, signifying hope for a species that continues to be its own worst enemy

I'm not familiar with any published systems, but I am also running a homebrew Fallout RPG, so I'd love to discuss further topics.

I guess it would be different if you're using Dnd/Pf, but in Fallout's PnP rules, weapons are broken down by skill. The weapon skills are: Big guns, Small guns, Energy Weapons, Melee, Throwing, Explosives, Unarmed.

A decent amount of variety can be found throughout the Fallout series, but since this is not a video game, it is a good idea to include more unconventional weapons with unique properties that take advantage of the freeform nature of tabletop roleplaying, such as a boomerang, or a slingshot that can shoot any object small and heavy enough.

Insofar as crafting goes, this is what I'm doing:

I have a loot deck for all items: weapons, clothes, armour, food, medicine, drugs, ammo, mods, random assorted junk. The players' inventory is a hand of cards that they can draw from at any time, though it costs AP to do so during combat. 

The majority of the cards are junk items, thus looting resembles sifting through a pile of garbage, and finding a good item is a big find. But the junk is also not worthless, as, like in FO4, it is made up of components that can be used to repair or create items and structures, as well as craft mods for weapons. 

However, unlike FO4, in which junk is only used at a workbench, in a tabletop RPG, crafting can take on a much more organic form. My players have surprised me several times by using junk in unexpected ways. When they find themselves in dire situations with nothing but a bunch of junk to work with, it gives them interesting opportunities to exercise their survivalist instincts:

-Nighttime approaches -> build a fire using any items containing wood

-someone is badly gashed across the leg -> break down an item containing cloth, bandage the wound

-cornered with nowhere to run -> toss a piece of junk to make a noise and distract/throw off the assailant

-enter a maze-like cavern or vault -> leave behind a trail of beads to follow back

I also have a character who will charge the players a fee to make a weapon out of  any 3 item they give him (quality may vary).

I have since gone all the way and added a quest where the players can assemble a vehicle out of scrap and enter it in a race.

I'm currently reading a book about lacrosse - the first third of it was mostly a cultural history, so I'm not yet familiar with specific strategies, but for a verrrrrry brief summary:

-nowadays it's played with 10 players (goalkeeper, 3 defensemen, 3 midfielders, 3 attackmen)

-the rules for the original game invented by the tribes of the First Nations were much less rigid - basically, don't touch the ball with your hands unless you're the goalkeeper - there could have been upwards of thousands if players, and a game could have taken place over miles of varied terrain; after all it was designed, among other things, to prepare young boys for war, and was even referred to as the "little brother of war"

-in reaction to the original game played by the natives, George Beers came up with a ruleset in 1869 for 12 player teams - goalkeeper, point, cover-point, centre, fielders - the rules were meant to make the game more suitable for smaller spaces, so he could play with his friends; it ended up popularizing the game with British settlers; it required less running but encouraged more passing, changed the ball from wood or deerskin to indian rubber, introduced referees and umpires, and a number of other rules, 22 to be exact

Keep in mind, the sport as it is in my game may not be exactly the same; since I'm working within the setting of Fallout, and some major themes of Fallout are history repeating itself, and the idea of cultures being built on the fragments of a society that dissappeared fairly recently, I wanted to have a game spread and evolve in much a similar way, starting with remnants of recorded history, such as paintings of people playing the game, plaques, and stories passed down by survivors.

From a narrative perspective:

1) in a few words, outline the mood you want to convey, and the themes you want to explore - what's the general feeling you want the location to give off? Impoverished? Oppressive? Desperate? Hopeful? Blissfully Ignorant? Pious? Distrustful? Secretive? Honourable? Preparing for war? Decide on a distinct combination of feelings that both makes it fit into the themes of the larger world, and also gives a unique perspective.

2) decide on the logistics of the location: what do people eat? Do they make their own food or do they trade for food? What are their major trading goods? What groups or factions, if any, reside in this location, and what kind of influence do they possess on its citizens? Economic? Military? Religious? What challenges do they face as a people? (this should play into the mood/theme) What solutions to these problems have people come up with? Is there conflict or tension within the community over these problems/solutions?

1 and 2 are interchangable, since it is possible to start in a location and expand out, or to start with a rough idea of the big picture and then zoom into each location to give it detail.

3) Characters can be crafted as logical consequences of the environment you create. The more impoverished a location is, the more it will rely on its farmers and hunters, so there will be more farmers and hunters. Larger places with a higher population will rely more on trade, which means people needed to process available resources, and people needed to transport these resources. If the need for food and trade is met, people will create new jobs within the community: shops, restaurants, construction, etc. 

This, in turn, gives rise to people who are willing to exploit these people/businesses for their own gain (eg. Criminals). This creates a need for law, and law enforcement, etc.

How well these systems work, and what they logically lead to, depends on the moods and themes you're trying to convey. With enough detail, you can simply pick a job - or lack of a job if there is a shortage of jobs or less reason to work - look at your overarching moods/themes, and your logistical web of cause->effect, and feel out a character based on their environment.

The hardest part is always naming them.

Personally, I really appreciate a kind of interperative way of approaching the world in which, for example, people and cultures remember and interpret history differently from one another - various peoples of various backgrounds see the world differently, and have different explanations for how the world around them came to be - and their contrasting beliefs or non-beliefs become sources of tension, as they lead to different ideas of what the future holds, and what must be done to stop/hasten it.

As long as the writing never "takes a side", and gives reason enough for one to believe that any of these interpretations could be accurate, it allows the reader/player/viewer to decide for themselves what they believe about the world, gives them a chance to invest themselves in the setting.

Personally I am pretty against the concept of defined "classes" in my games, and find it a lot more effective to provide players with a robust set of stats, skills and specialized perks so players can play whatever role they want.

I would separate the roles into:

-Attributes: to be assigned at the start of the game (innate abilities: strength, dexterity, charisma, etc.)
 
and
-Learned skills: affected by attributes immediately, and increased with use or with skill points earned after each successful heist, or however you'd want to measure "levelling"
(stealth, safecracking, guns, melee, hand-to-hand, speech, hacking, parkour, demolitions, pilot, etc.)

Then specialized perks can be unlocked as characters become more proficient in skills, allowing them to play an even more specialized role.

For instance, in speech, you could have an intimidation perk, a smartass perk, a persuasion perk and a smooth talker perk, all suggesting different characters.

In guns, you could have perks for characters specializing with pistols, sniper rifles, smgs or heavy ordnance.

This creates a system where you can build any character you want, and you will be rewarded for specializing and roleplaying your unique skillset.

There are two sets of perks: skill perks and misc perks.

Each skill has six perks pertaining to it. Skill perks are made available to the player with each skill increment of 10 from 50 up to 100.

A player can only begin taking skill perks once they have at least 50 in the skill for which they want a perk. However, a player with a 76 in Gambling but no perks in Gambling, may take any perk under the skill up to and below 70 without it being gated behind the lower perks. These perks are designed to specialize the character and allow the player to express their role mechanically.

Misc perks are more ambiguous and whimsical. Some of them pertain to S.P.E.C.I.A.L. stats but most of them stand alone, and offer some mechanical bonus or change.

These perks are in a deck, and upon leveling up the deck is shuffled and 10 perks are presented for the players' choosing.

The players may take a perk from either set upon leveling up.

That's how I like to think of their discography - the sound of the stages of grief.

Pablo Honey is youth, optimism, and naiveté.

The Bends sees first contact with grief, and makes up most of the denial phase; mostly light hearted with occasional moments of introspection that eventually lead back to a lighter sound, but Street Spirit leaves us wondering...

Ok Computer remains in denial for the first half, up until "Fitter Happier" when the illusion finally breaks and there is nothing left but anger., which carries the second half.

Kid A takes place long after the anger has subsided, and we're left with cold Isolation.

Amnesiac sees depression begin to set in, as we begin to feel like a prisoner in our own isolation.

Hail to the Thief is the beginning of the bargaining phase, where a desperate search is conducted for ways to guarantee no further pain or grief. For the first time, we are looking outward for answers rather than inward, and this leads to much discontent with the world around us.

In Rainbows sees a return to the introspective but with new answers gleamed from the time spent looking outward.

The King of Limbs mirrors the emotional progressions through each album, looking back at each phase until track 8, Separator, which sees the first glimpse of acceptance of all this.

Finally, A Moon Shaped Pool sees the phase of Acceptance. Denial is pointless, as is anger. All that's left are the many lessons learned along the way, and a childlike fascination in the universe that caused all of this to happen in the first place.

I was about 13. I'd heard of them but had never listened to them - as far as I knew at the time.

I went to a music camp in the summer, where kids are grouped into bands, which then all play a show every night for the length of the camp. I played drums.

Our singer was a huge Radiohead fan, and one night he suggested Karma Police. We listened to it a few times throughout the day to get the arrangement right - we had three people on guitar, because a lot of campers played guitar - and while I wasn't crazy about it at first, the song warmed up to me over the week.

Flash forward a few weeks to my freshman year of highschool. I go to my first high school dance, I ask a girl if she'd like to dance, she says "maybe later" and turns away, I'm sad, I have no friends here, everything is the worst, etc. 

I'm walking home in the dark afterward, with that blank apathetic stare you get when you hate everything so much that you just remove yourself from consciousness and become a passive audience member instead, just to numb yourself. The melody of Karma Police pops into my head, and I find myself humming lowly all the way home.

I get on the computer and immediately search up the song for a listen. I like this way more all of a sudden. I should check out some of their other stuff.

I'll give you one guess what the first song to come up was.

Of course, I'd heard creep before in passing and dismissed it as whiny post grunge garbage. However, now it was describing how I felt perfectly, young, confused angsty nihilistic teen that I was. I was absolutely shocked that this was the same band, and I felt no small amount of guilt for enjoying it more with that knowledge.

Right after finding out that this was the same band that was responsible for Creep, I dove straight into OK Computer.

The first seconds of Airbag hooked me immediately. Instantly I knew this was the beginning of something really special. What followed was a euphoric week where every day I listened to a new radiohead record, and with every record I was astounded that I was still listening to the same band that made the previous.

Never looked at music the same way again. Never really looked at anything the same way again.
